title: Bat Mortality and Activity at a Northern Iowa Wind Resource Area
abstract: We examined bat collision mortality, activity and species composition at an 89turbine wind resource area in farmland of north-central Iowa from mid-Apr. to mid-Dec., 2003 and mid-Mar. to mid-Dec., 2004. We found 30 bats beneath turbines on cleared ground and gravel access areas in 2003 and 45 bats in 2004. After adjusting for search probability, search efficiency and scavenging rate, we estimated total bat mortality at 396 6 72 (95% CI) in 2003 and 636 6 112 (95% CI) in 2004. Although carcasses were mostly migratory tree bats, we found a considerable proportion of little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus). We recorded 1465 bat echolocation call files at turbine sites (x 5 34.88 call files/detector-night) and 1536 bat call files at adjacent non-turbine sites (x 5 36.57 call files/detector-night). Bat activity did not differ significantly between turbine and non-turbine sites. A large proportion of recorded call files were made by Myotis sp. but this may be because we detected activity at ground level only. There was no relationship between types of turbine lights and either collision mortality or echolocation activity. The highest levels of bat echolocation activity and collision mortality were recorded during Jul. and Aug. during the autumn dispersal and migration period. The fatality rates for bats in general and little brown bats in particular were higher at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area than at other, comparable studies in the region. Future efforts to study behavior of bats in flight around turbines as well as cumulative impact studies should not ignore non-tree dwelling bats, generally regarded as minimally affected.

## Bat Mortality and Activity at a Northern Iowa Wind Resource Area

AAFTAB A. JAIN[1]

Iowa Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Department of Natural Resource Ecology and Management, Iowa State University, Ames 50011

## ROLF R. KOFORD

U.S. Geological Survey, Iowa Cooperative Fish and Wildlife Research Unit, Iowa State University, Ames 50011

## AND

## ALAN W. HANCOCK AND GUY G. ZENNER

Iowa Department of Natural Resources, 1203 North Shore Drive, Clear Lake 50428

ABSTRACT.—We examined bat collision mortality, activity and species composition at an 89turbine wind resource area in farmland of north-central Iowa from mid-Apr. to mid-Dec., 2003 and mid-Mar. to mid-Dec., 2004. We found 30 bats beneath turbines on cleared ground and gravel access areas in 2003 and 45 bats in 2004. After adjusting for search probability, search efficiency and scavenging rate, we estimated total bat mortality at 396 6 72 (95% CI) in 2003 and 636 6 112 (95% CI) in 2004. Although carcasses were mostly migratory tree bats, we found a considerable proportion of little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus). We recorded 1465 bat echolocation call files at turbine sites ( **x** 5 34.88 call files/detector-night) and 1536 bat call files at adjacent non-turbine sites ( **x** 5 36.57 call files/detector-night). Bat activity did not differ significantly between turbine and non-turbine sites. A large proportion of recorded call files were made by Myotis sp. but this may be because we detected activity at ground level only. There was no relationship between types of turbine lights and either collision mortality or echolocation activity. The highest levels of bat echolocation activity and collision mortality were recorded during Jul. and Aug. during the autumn dispersal and migration period. The fatality rates for bats in general and little brown bats in particular were higher at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area than at other, comparable studies in the region. Future efforts to study behavior of bats in flight around turbines as well as cumulative impact studies should not ignore non-tree dwelling bats, generally regarded as minimally affected.

## INTRODUCTION

Wind power is a financially competitive source of electricity in the USA that is generally viewed as having few negative effects on the environment. Recent studies have found large numbers of bats killed beneath wind turbines (Fiedler et al., 2002; Kerns and Kerlinger, 2004; Arnett, 2005). As differing methods of mortality estimation are being concurrently developed and adopted by research institutions, consulting firms and state and federal agencies (Arnett et al., 2009; Gritski et al., 2009), Kunz et al. (2007) highlighted the need to employ scientifically valid, post-construction monitoring protocols to ensure comparable results across different sites and to conduct full-season multi-year post-construction monitoring studies to assess species composition and abundance, as well as temporal and spatial patterns of bat activity at facilities that encompass diverse landscapes. While less alarming fatality levels have been found in other regional wind resource areas (WRA), the

wildlife management areas (WMA) in close proximity to this WRA act as a unique resource for wildlife in an otherwise highly agricultural region. Higher fatality rates or unusual species composition of fatalities would strongly affect future consideration of ecologically sensitive areas for wind resource development.

The Top of Iowa WRA was constructed in Dec. 2001 in Worth County in north-central Iowa, in a general agricultural matrix (primarily corn and soybeans) with nearby woodlands and wetlands in the surrounding region that could provide roosting and feeding habitat for bats. This landscape context provided an opportunity to estimate the amount of collision mortality and to gain insight into how bats interact with a WRA-influenced environment. We conducted a study from 15 Apr. to 15 Dec. 2003 and from 15 Mar. to 15 Dec. 2004, to assess the collision mortality of bats at the Top of Iowa WRA and to characterize bat activity in the region. Study objectives included estimating the number of bat fatalities due to turbine collisions, comparing bat echolocation activity between areas with wind turbines and adjacent crop fields, and describing any trends in bat activity and mortality related to seasonal, weather and habitat-related factors.

## METHODS

## STUDY AREA

This study was conducted at the Top of Iowa WRA, Worth County, Iowa, an 89-turbine wind farm completed in late 2001 and encompassing 2137 ha. Besides the aforementioned primary vegetation types, minor habitat types included hay, Conservation Reserve Program (CRP) grassland and deciduous woodlots associated with farmsteads. The wind farm was located among three WMAs that were complexes of wetland, grassland and wooded habitat (Fig. 1). While no data exist on the historic use of this site by bats, the close proximity to three WMAs and many farmsteads likely provides habitat for bats that roost in both trees and man-made structures. The wind turbines were mounted on 71.6 m high tubular towers and turned by three 25.9 m blades with a 2107.69 m[2] sweep area. Forty-six turbines were lit at the top of the nacelle with Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) non-blinking red beacons. Thirty-seven turbines situated on the periphery of the wind farm had blinking red beacons. Because of their proximity to the Lake Mills Municipal Airport, six turbines in the northwest corner of the wind facility had a combination of blinking white beacons and non-blinking red beacons. In addition to wind towers, there are two (71.6 m high) guyed towers on site, which gather meteorological data for the Top of Iowa WRA.

## MORTALITY

We looked for evidence of collision-induced mortality under 26 of 89 wind turbines, from 15 Apr. to 15 Dec. 2003 and from 15 Mar. to 15 Dec. 2004, spanning the entire season of expected bat activity in Iowa over a multi-year project. We used a stratified, randomized design. The WRA occupied 35 sections of 2.59 km[2] each. To randomize within each section, we eliminated six sections that contained only one turbine. The remaining 29 sections were divided into 14 pairs of adjacent sections and one additional section. We randomly selected two towers from each pair, as well as two additional turbines from the additional section, for a total of 30 turbines selected. Thus, we ensured adequate geographic distribution of mortality sampling sites through the study area, while retaining an element of randomization. Landowner permission to access sites was received for 26 out of the 30 turbines selected. The remaining four turbines were eliminated from the study. In 2003, a tenant farmer revoked permission for one of the 26 searched turbines, 2 mo into the study. Within a month, we set up a substitute turbine search site in a neighboring section.

FIG. 1.—Location of the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area (light shading), Worth County, Iowa, relative to nearby Wildlife Management Areas (dark shading). Worth County, Iowa. Dots indicate tower locations

Each of the selected turbines had a 76-m by 76-m easement centered on the turbine. We kept six, 3 m-wide, 76 m-long transects free of vegetation, using herbicides and manual weeding (Anderson et al., 1999), under each of the 26 selected turbines. For each turbine, transects ran parallel to existing corn/soybean rows and were at random distances from the base of the turbine (three transects on either side of the turbine). We randomized transect locations again in 2004, except for three turbines where we retained the 2003 transects, as existing corn stubble made clearing new transects ineffective. We also searched the entire area of access roads and construction pads that were within the 76 m by 76 m square under each turbine. The average total area searched under each turbine was 1742 m[2] which was about 30% of the 5776 m[2] search plot. Standardized searches of all transects began 15 Apr. 2003, immediately after transects were set up. Initially, we searched each turbine once every 3 d. However, we had the capacity to complete more searches per day and from 13 Jun. 2003 the search frequency increased to once every 2 d, until the end of the season, 15 Dec. 2003. This change occurred before the late summer/autumn period when the majority of incidents were noted, thus did not affect our final estimates of mortality. Starting 15 Mar. 2004, the mortality study sites were reestablished and 2 d cycle standardized searches of all mortality transects began on 24 Mar. 2004 and continued through 15 Dec. 2004.

FIG. 2.—Overhead view of area searched under each meteorological tower in 2004, comprising two adjacent transects under each of the three sets of guy wires, at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area, Worth County, Iowa

We collected and froze all bat carcasses found during searches for later species identification and necropsy at the Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory at Iowa State University. Carcasses were examined for evidence of collision trauma and for body condition such as muscle mass, fat reserves and presence of food in the gut. We froze carcasses within 3 h of recovery.

We also collected carcasses found at other times, such as when visiting turbine sites for other aspects of the project and while walking between search transects. However, similar to Johnson et al. (2003), we did not include these carcasses in our estimated total mortality at the site because the detection area associated with them was unknown. In addition, during 2004 we searched under the two meteorological towers. We searched 3.05-m wide transects on either side of the guy wires, from the base of the tower to the point where the guy wires anchored in the ground. The total area searched under each meteorological tower was 881.76 m[2] (Fig. 2).

Adjusting for search probability, carcass retention while exposed to scavengers, search efficiency and proportion of turbines searched.—We estimated mortality for the entire WRA using a two-step process to adjust the number of fatalities found in the searched area. First, the number of fatalities found on the transects (C) was adjusted to account for the fact that some fatalities may have been in cropland between transects and hence not found. At each of the 26 turbines searched, we recorded the location of each fatality and its distance to the turbine using a Global Positioning System and geographic information system (GIS) software (ArcView 3.3). The distribution of fatalities may not have been uniform over the entire 5776 m[2] search plot. Therefore, we defined six concentric buffers of 10-m width, centered on each turbine, and calculated the proportion of each buffer that was searched (p). Assuming that fatality location was unrelated to whether the ground was vegetated or clear transect, we created a mortality estimate (t) for each buffer, where t 5 C/p. We calculated the variance of this estimate across buffers for each of the turbines searched. We summed the estimates and variances of t over 26 turbines to produce an estimate (T ) and variance of the number of fatalities for all searched turbines.

In addition, the number of bat fatalities in each buffer, divided by the area searched within that buffer, also provided a measure of Incident Density (Id ) in our transects. We used this metric to assess whether our search area was adequate to retrieve all collision incidents.

In the next step, we adjusted the estimate (T ) for carcass retention (R ) while exposed to scavengers, search efficiency (E ) of observers and the proportion of turbines on the wind farm that were searched (P ).

- (a) Carcass retention while exposed to scavengers (R ). We measured the proportion of test carcasses left by scavengers within the search period during spring, summer and late autumn of 2003 and 2004 by placing small birds, of house sparrow (Passer domesticus) size, on mortality transects under each of the 26 monitored wind turbines. The retention rate was expected to be high due to the short (2 d) search cycle. Thus, the rate as estimated with small birds would be similar to that of bats. Subsequent studies where both birds and bats have been used (Jain et al., 2007, 2008, 2009a, b, c) found similar rates of carcass retention, over a period of 1 d, between small birds and bats. In 2003 we placed nine trial carcasses each on 27 May, 15 Jul. and 28 Nov., respectively. In 2004 we placed 9, 9 and 10 trial carcasses on 1 Jun., 15 Jul. and 30 Nov., respectively. We placed carcasses in predetermined positions in mortality transects, so that there would be no confusion between test carcasses and other carcasses found on transects. We monitored carcasses daily for 2 wk for evidence of scavenging. We recorded the status of each carcass as intact, partially scavenged or completely removed. After the 2 wk period, we collected and disposed of all remaining carcasses. With a 2 d search interval, the expected time a carcass is available to be found is the mean time between the time the carcass appeared (distributed over the 2 d) and the next search event. The mean time between the appearance and the end of the interval would be approximately 1 d, assuming either a random or uniform distribution of appearances during the interval. Thus, we calculated R by dividing the number of carcasses remaining after 1 d by the total number of scavenged test carcasses (similar to methods described and reviewed in Smallwood [2007]).

- (b) Percentage of carcasses found by observers in the search efficiency trials (E ). Search efficiency trials were conducted for each observer by having an independent Iowa Department of Natural Resources wildlife technician place small birds, such as house sparrows, on transects without the searchers’ knowledge. Small birds were used due to the lack of availability of sufficient bats to conduct trials. The bat species observed ranged in color from dull brown [big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus), eastern pipistrelle bats (Perimyotis subflavus) and little brown bats (Myotis lucifugus)] and dark black (silverhaired bats, Lasionycteris noctivagans) to the brighter hoary bat (Lasiurus cinereus) and eastern red bat (L. borealis). Similarly, the birds used were mostly inconspicuous with dull brown, black and gray bodies and gray underbodies. A few birds may have been slightly larger than the smaller bat species; however, bats may have been more uniform in shading, making them easier to pick out. We believed these differences largely cancelled out when comparing test bird carcasses to the range of bat species found. In addition, subsequent studies where both birds and bats have been used (Jain et al., 2007, 2008, 2009a, b, c) found similar search efficiency rates between small birds and bats. The observers recorded all evidence of carcasses they discovered, including carcasses planted by the independent wildlife technician. Planted carcasses later were removed from the database and a search efficiency rate (E ) calculated (number of carcasses found divided by the total number of test carcasses).

- (c) In addition, we adjusted the estimate for the proportion of turbines that we searched relative to the total number of turbines on the study area (P ). _ T

The variance of the number of fatalities found in the searched areas (T ) was discussed earlier. The variances for R and E were first calculated per turbine using standard methods for proportions, i.e., Var (x)~1⁄2(x)(1{x)=n, where n was the number of test carcasses and x was either carcasses retained or carcasses found (Ramsey and Schafer, 2002). The proportion P was a constant. Thus, we calculated the variance due to the correction factors R, E and P by combining formulas for the variances of the product of a constant and a random variable and the product of two random variables (Goodman, 1960).

BAT ACTIVITY

We used two bat echolocation detectors (Anabat II H, Titley Electronics Pty. Ltd., NSW, Australia, www.titley.com.au) attached to Compact Flash Storage Zero-Crossings Analysis Interface Modules (ZCAIM) to collect ultrasonic bat passes at the bases of wind turbine sites as well as in adjacent fields without wind turbines. The ZCAIM stores data sent by the detector in individual files distinguished by intervening periods of no ultrasonic detection. We eliminated files that did not contain at least one call as well as all files that contained only background noise and then counted each file as a separate pass. We conducted a pilot study of bat activity in 2003, using the bat detectors to monitor bat activity for a short duration, from 4 Sep. 2003 to 9 Oct. 2003 (14 detector-nights). We performed a full-season study the following year, from 26 May 2004 to 24 Sep. 2004 (84 detector-nights). We waterproofed the detectors for passive monitoring (O’Farrell, 1998) and left them to record activity from sunset to sunrise at each site. We systematically sampled 14 of the 26 turbines searched for bat carcasses (see Mortality section of Methods), by placing a detector away from the electric transformer, backing the base of turbines, pointed upward at a slight angle (30u from horizontal). We placed a second detector at the edge of an adjacent field, in a paired design. We used adjacent field edges rather than locations in the centers of fields to ensure that farming activity did not damage detectors. The landscape around the Top of Iowa WRA was mostly uniform agricultural land. Most (10) field edge detector sites were on boundaries between adjacent corn or soy fields, defined by a low mound of vegetation or a wire fence. Three edge sites had a small number of trees (1–5) typical of the region. We did not have access to place the detectors at any height on the turbine towers, or in adjacent fields. However, data collected reflect relative activity close to and away from turbines. We downloaded digital data collected by the bat detectors each day.

Turbine versus non-turbine activity.—We analyzed differences between total passes recorded at turbine versus adjacent sites with a paired t-test using PROC GLM (SAS Institute Inc, 2001). We used software programs Analook (O’Farrell, 1998) and Analyze ( Jolly, 1997) to identify bats based on their echolocation passes and thus estimate relative activity of each species. After eliminating files that did not contain at least one bat call, we counted each file that the ZCAIM software defined (Britzke et al., 1999) as a unit of activity. We used a species identification key (K. Francl, University of Notre Dame, pers. comm.) to determine species for a seasonal subset of bat passes recorded. This key was designed to differentiate between

the following species: hoary bats, silver-haired bats, big brown bats, evening bats (Nycticeius humeralis), northern myotis (Myotis septentrionalis), little brown bats and the combined group of eastern red bats and eastern pipistrelles. No other bat species were expected in this region of north-central Iowa (Barbour and Davis, 1969). We analyzed passes recorded over days from late spring (5 May 2004 to 26 May 2004) and late summer/early autumn (29 Jul. 2004 to 26 Aug. 2004) to sample bat activity in both spring and autumn migratory seasons. For species analysis, we discarded passes if they contained fewer than two individual calls (Britzke et al., 1999). Where possible, we identified passes to species. We used known bat passes from bat pass libraries supplied by K. Francl to test the identification key for accuracy.

Distance to nearest woodlot.—We used a GIS (ArcView 3.3, Environmental Systems Research Institute, Inc., Redlands, California) to estimate the distance of the nearest woodlot to each turbine monitored by use of 2002 infrared ortho-photos at 1 m[2] resolution. We examined the relationship between bat activity and distance to nearest woodlot and to the nearest WMA using a multiple linear regression model in which the number of passes was the response variable and distances to the nearest woodlot and WMAs were explanatory variables.

Turbine lights.—Bats have been known to forage for insects attracted to artificial lighting (Acharya and Fenton, 1999). We examined the relationship between bat activity and turbine lights. Four turbine sites with red blinking beacons were among the 13 sites monitored for bat activity. Eight turbine sites with non-blinking red beacons also were monitored. As an artifact of sampling from the mortality phase of the project, only one turbine of the third light type (red non-blinking and white-dual blinking lights) was sampled for bat activity, therefore, was not included in the following analysis. We used ANOVA to test for a difference between bat activity at turbines of red blinking and non-blinking beacon types (PROC GLM, SAS Institute Inc, 2001). We also used ANOVA to test for a difference between the (log) numbers of bat carcasses found under turbines of each beacon type (PROC GLM, SAS Institute Inc, 2001). We conducted mortality searches under 13 turbines lit with blinking red beacons, four turbines with dual red non-blinking beacons and blinking white beacons and nine with non-blinking red beacons.

Wind speed.—We obtained maximum wind speeds, during the inter-search periods in which bat collisions occurred, from one of the two 71.6 m high meteorological towers on site, to identify any important wind events that may have coincided with a mortality event. The meteorological towers were located at the northwestern and southern ends of the wind farm, approximately 150 m from the nearest wind tower, within the same field. Data were collected at 1700, 2100 and 0300 h.

## RESULTS

In 2003, we found the carcasses or partial remains of 30 bats within the designated search area (11 hoary, 9 little brown, 5 eastern red, 3 big brown and 2 silver-haired bats). An additional eastern red bat was found incidentally, between transects. Other than one silverhaired bat that we found in the spring (Apr.), all bats were found from Jun. to Oct. (Fig. 3). In 2004, we found the carcasses or partial remains of 45 bats (11 hoary, 13 eastern red, 8 little brown, 5 big brown, 7 silver-haired and 1 eastern pipistrelle bat). An additional eastern red bat was found incidentally, under a turbine that did not have a designated search area. Neither of the incidental finds were in cleared search areas and so were not included in our mortality estimates. We found all carcasses in summer or autumn, from Jun. to Sep. 2004 (Fig. 3). We did not find any bats under the meteorological towers searched in 2004.

FIG. 3.—Distribution of bat mortality by month, observed over 2003 and 2004, at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area, Worth County, Iowa

Of 30 bat carcasses recovered in 2003 and analyzed at the Veterinary Diagnostic Laboratory, 23 were in good enough physical condition for necropsy. Nineteen (,83%) showed obvious signs of trauma, typically bone fractures and hemorrhaging, whereas the remaining four carcasses (,17%) did not. However, of these four, the veterinarian performing the necropsy rated two carcasses in poor/marginal state of preservation. Out of the 45 bat carcasses recovered in 2004, 33 were in good enough physical condition to necropsy. Twenty-two (,67%) showed obvious signs of trauma, whereas the remaining 11 carcasses (,33%) did not. However, most (seven) of the carcasses that did not show an apparent cause of death were rated in poor state of preservation in the necropsy report, which stated that ‘‘Decomposition may have obscured many of the more subtle internal lesions, and only the most dramatic traumatic lesions were discernable’’ (M Yaeger, pers. comm.). Although we searched sites approximately once every 2 d, small body sizes, warm ambient temperatures and insect activity quickly degraded the physical condition of the bats. For all carcasses where mortality could not be attributed to collision, no evidence of poor muscle mass or fat reserves accompanied with lack of food in gut was observed. Where possible we eliminated disease or starvation as obvious causes of death. Given the lack of alternate causes of death, and/or the poor condition of these carcasses, we attributed them to turbine collisions.

Two of the 19 carcasses in 2003 that showed evidence of trauma had internal thoracic hemorrhage without other evidence of physical trauma, similar to the phenomenon of barotrauma described by Baerwald et al. (2008). No such carcasses were found in 2004. Combining the results from both years, a much lower proportion of carcasses that underwent necropsy (20.0%, n 5 15) showed no obvious signs of collision trauma than the

46.28% as reported in Baerwald et al. (2008). As most bats showed signs of collision trauma, we did not suspect alternate causes of wind turbine related fatality such as barotrauma, nor did we conduct histological examinations or specifically check for lung damage as did Baerwald et al. (2008).

Adjusting for search probability, carcass retention and search efficiency.—We pooled data from spring, summer and autumn scavenging trials within each year as the level of scavenging did not differ significantly among seasons in either 2003 (x[2] 5 2.34, df 5 25, P 5 0.31) or 2004 (x[2] 5 0.35, df 5 26, P 5 0.84). Spring, summer and autumn scavenging trials indicated scavengers left an average of 93% (25/27) and 89% (25/28) of small bird carcasses within the interval between searches in this study, in 2003 and 2004 respectively. Observer efficiency trials revealed that, as a group, observers found 71% (27/38) and 74% (26/35) of small bird carcasses in 2003 and 2004, respectively. The ratios of the area searched to the total area (p) for buffers 1–6 under the 26 turbines were 0.84, 0.41, 0.34, 0.30, 0.26 and 0.17 in 2003 and 0.83, 0.44, 0.35, 0.29, 0.23 and 0.13 in 2004.

Using the estimate of C_ and its variance, adjusted estimates of bat mortality for the Top of Iowa WRA were 396.05 6 71.71 (95% CI) bats (4.45 bats/turbine, 4.94 bats/MW) between 15 Apr. 2003 and 15 Dec. 2003 and 635.83 6 111.89 (95% CI) bats (7.14 bats/turbine, 7.94 bats/MW) between 24 Mar. 2004 and 15 Dec. 2004.

Incident density.—We examined the density of found incidents (Id) and related it to distance from the tower (Fig. 5). One incident out of 75, which was found in the outermost buffer, would have generated an outlier density estimate and was not used in this analysis.

Turbine lights.—No significant difference in bat mortality was observed between turbines with the three different types of FAA lighting (F2,23 5 1.42, P 5 0.26).

Wind speed.—Maximum wind speeds during the inter-search periods in which bat collisions occurred ranged from 2.4 m/sec to 4.9 m/sec in 2003 and 2.7 m/sec to 5.3 m/sec in 2004.

## BAT ACTIVITY

We recorded bat activity for 84 detector-nights (in 2004). We detected 1465 bat call files at turbine sites ( ̄ **x** 5 34.88 per detector-night, over 42 nights) and 1536 bat call files at nonturbine sites ( ̄ **x** 5 36.57 per detector-night over 42 nights). As we had one detector at a turbine and non-turbine site each, one night of detection resulted in two detector-nights worth of data. We recorded echolocation activity at all of the sites monitored. The maximum number of call files recorded in one night at one detector was 245 call files on 12 Sep. 2004 at a non-turbine site and 195 call files on 29 Jun. 2004 at a turbine site. Bat activity in 2004, measured by the number of call files per night (Fig. 4), peaked in Jul. (99.5 call files/ detector-night) and Aug. (56.44 call files/detector-night). Bat activity was lower in Sept. (10.5 call files/detector-night) and had mostly ceased by Oct., when detection was curtailed. This followed a trend similar to mortality which also was highest in Jul. and Aug. (Fig. 4).

The 2003 pilot study using Anabat ultrasonic bat detectors indicated no significant difference between bat activity at wind turbine sites and adjacent crop fields without turbines (F1,12 5 0.24, P 5 0.63). The 2004 study (May to Sept. 2004) also found no significant difference between bat activity at wind turbine sites and adjacent crop fields without turbines (F1,70 5 0.07, P 5 0.78). Analysis of the 2004 data showed no significant effect of distance to nearest woodlot (t10 5 0.86, P 5 0.41), or WMA (t10 5 20.97, P 5 0.35 ) on the number of bat calls recorded at different turbines. There was also no significant difference between the number of calls recorded at turbines with red blinking and nonblinking beacons (F1,10 5 0.07, P 5 0.79).

FIG. 4.—Average bat-calling activity per turbine-night and bat mortality in each month of the active season at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area, Worth County, Iowa (Apr.–Sep. 2004)

Qualitative analysis.—From our examination of known bat passes using the species identification key, we were confident that we would able to differentiate Myotis sp. from calls of other species with ,80% certainty. The remaining species were not easily differentiable. As all Myotis fatalities were little brown bats, we presumed that calls identified as Myotis also most likely were little brown bats. In the late spring/early summer subset of calls analyzed, we identified 44% of calls as little brown bats (out of 45 calls over nine detector-nights). In the autumn subset of calls, we identified 40% of calls as little brown bats (out of 595 calls recorded over 11 detector-nights). The low number of calls analyzed in the spring subset as compared with the autumn subset reflected lower levels of detected bat activity.

## DISCUSSION

As the impacts of WRAs are likely to vary by region, comparisons among studies must consider regional differences among habitat, wildlife abundance and behavior as well as differences in study methods. Our estimated mortality rates were higher than those of other WRA studies in the Midwest (Osborn et al., 1996; Howe et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2003, 2004). Subsequent studies in the eastern U.S. (Arnett et al., 2008) showed fatality rates ranging from 20–70 fatalities per turbine per year. Higher fatality rates at wind farms on forested ridge tops in the east reflect the greater availability of wooded area for bats. See Arnett et al. (2008) for a comprehensive discussion of bat collision mortality at WRAs in North America.

Estimators of collision mortality vary among projects and researchers and can introduce inadvertent bias into results (Smallwood, 2007). New estimators are currently being developed that can better adjust for search efficiency and scavenging, but further improvements are necessary. Other studies (Johnson et al., 2003, 2004) have used carcass persistence time as an estimator for scavenging, whereas we used percent of carcasses

FIG. 5.—Density of mortality incidents relative to distance from the base of searched towers at the Top of Iowa Wind Resource Area, Worth County, Iowa, from sites searched in 2003 and 2004

remaining over the search cycle, similar to methods described and recommended in Smallwood (2007). Persistence time typically is estimated over a period of at least 2 wk (Erickson et al., 2002). However, the shorter search duration of this study (2 d) versus seven, 14 and even 30 d search cycles in other studies makes ‘percent of carcasses remaining’ a more appropriate metric. Persistence time averaged over the course of a weekly scavenge study would not well reflect the amount of scavenging that occurs in a short, 2 d search cycle. However, our estimator model presumes that all carcasses not found during a search cycle do not remain to be found in subsequent searches, which may not always be the case. Further improvements in the estimator model are needed to adjust for this deficiency, which may currently overestimate fatality. This adjustment is negligibly useful in studies with a longer search cycle or with higher scavenge rates.

We estimated search efficiency and scavenge rates by the use of small birds, as bat carcasses were not available. Johnson (2002, 2004) reported higher search efficiencies for bats than small birds (,30% for small birds and ,47% for bats). Search efficiency varied with substrate searched in those and other studies (Anderson et al., 1999; Morrison, 2002). It seems reasonable that the bare ground transects at the Top of Iowa WRA would reduce the differences between search efficiency for small birds and bats. Similar protocols in later studies (Jain et al., 2007, 2009b, c) in New York did not show a tendency of higher search efficiency for bats compared to small birds in four out of five study-years. In four out of five studies, the difference between bird and bat search efficiency rates ranged from 0 to 10% (median 5 5%). In the one study where the difference in rates was similar to Johnson (2002, 2004), small bird search efficiency was greater than bat search efficiency.

Our search transects were distributed to sample an area within at least a 38 m radius from the base of each turbine. Johnson et al. (2003) found 0.5% of bat carcasses .33 m from turbines that attained a maximum rotor height of 73 m, compared to the Top of Iowa WRA turbines that reached a maximum rotor height of 98 m. Our data (Fig. 5) showed an immediate drop in carcass density outside a 10 m circle from the base of the tower. However, the density, while low, did not drop to zero at the outer limits of our search area,

indicating that it is possible that some carcasses landed farther from turbines than we searched, making our final estimate somewhat lower than if we could have searched farther from the tower base.

Several factors may cause bats to be susceptible to collision with wind turbines; local and regional habitat, population levels, flight height, weather and visibility conditions, turbine lighting and use of the regions immediately around the turbines.

Local habitat.—It is possible that bat activity at the Top of Iowa WRA was affected by local habitat availability, including the three WMAs near the wind farm and likely food resources in nearby woodlots and farmsteads that could provide additional local habitat for bats (Barbour and Davis, 1969; Mager and Nelson, 2001). Anabat detectors placed below turbines recorded a greater number of bat passes (34.88 passes/turbine/night) in this study compared to 1–2 passes/turbine/night recorded below turbines at the Buffalo Ridge WRA using similar methodologies (Johnson et al., 2004). The lower measure of passes corresponds to a lower fatality rate estimated at that wind farm (3.02 and 1.30 fatalities per turbine) indicating that activity detected by Anabat systems may have some use as an indicator of fatalities (Baerwald and Barclay, 2009). However, experimental study design and use of detectors at turbine height would provide more useful results.

Unlike Johnson et al. (2004) in Minnesota, we did not find a negative relationship between distance to nearest woodlot and bat activity, nor did we find a significant relationship between distance to nearest WMA and bat activity. Further, bat activity did not differ at turbine and non-turbine sites, so we have no evidence that the presence of wind turbines was associated with avoidance behavior.

Species composition.—Previous studies in the Midwest have hypothesized that higher numbers of hoary, eastern red and silver-haired bat collisions observed probably were due to their long-range migratory behavior (Erickson et al., 2002; Johnson et al., 2003, 2004; Arnett et al., 2008). However, hoary bats at the Top of Iowa WRA were killed in the greatest numbers in both 2003 and 2004, whereas they composed only ,29% (22/75) of the total kills over both years. Fatalities of summer-resident species, including little brown and big brown bats, were reported as usually low (0–13.5%) across North America (Arnett et al., 2007). The proportion of fatalities of summer residents reported at the Top of Iowa WRA was much higher (,33% little brown and big brown bats). Little brown bats exhibit some migratory behavior, traveling to hibernacula up to 150–450 km from their summer roosts (Barbour and Davis, 1969), which may increase collision risk through an increase in encounter rates with wind turbines as a function of increased migration length. If bat migratory flight occurs at greater heights than foraging, this would further increase risk of collisions, but little is known of this behavior (Baerwald and Barclay, 2009). Spring and summer acoustic surveys at the Top of Iowa WRA revealed that Myotis sp., possibly little brown bats, made up approximately 40–44% of recorded species.

Turbine lighting.—Some species of bats forage for insects attracted to artificial lights (McClure, 1939, 1942; Acharya and Fenton, 1999). As all turbines at the Top of Iowa WRA had FAA lights, we could not test for differences in mortality or activity between lit and unlit turbines. However, we found no effect of the type of turbine lighting (red blinking and nonblinking beacons and white strobe lights) on mortality or activity. Johnson et al. (2004), Fiedler et al. (2007) and Jain et al. (2009a, b, c) also did not find a significant difference in mortality between lit and unlit turbines.

Weather.—No individual mortality event coincided with a major storm or unusually high winds, in either 2003 or 2004. The peak season for wind-related energy production is spring. As all mortality except for one bat occurred in summer and autumn, high winds were not an

obvious cause of mortality. Maximum wind speeds during the inter-search periods in which bat collisions occurred were less than 6 m/sec. Kerns and Kerlinger (2004) and Johnson et al. (2004) found no correlation between weather events and collision mortality. Fiedler et al. (2007) and Arnett (2005) found evidence of greater numbers of bat collisions at lower wind speeds. While we did not test for that relationship, our data do not contradict their findings.

Seasonal trends.—Kunz et al. (2007) described uncertainty with respect to the seasonality of bat fatalities in North America due to less intensive search efforts in the spring and summer periods. However, our data reflect a full-season, multi-year monitoring study that include spring and autumn migratory periods and summer months when bats are in residence. The very low number of bats found in the spring and summer months cannot be due to our slightly lower search effort in the first two months in 2003 (3 d search frequency). Further, our search effort in 2004 did not vary at all between seasons. Finally, similar trends have been seen at other study sites with similar methods (Arnett et al., 2008; Jain et al., 2007, 2008).

Although we did not test for significance, the seasonal increase in bat acoustic activity closely preceded the overall incidence of fatalities and corresponded with the post-breeding southward migration for hoary, eastern red and silver-haired bats (Cryan, 2003), as well as the timing of movement from summer breeding areas to hibernacula for big brown, little brown and eastern pipistrelle bats (Barclay, 1984; Genter and Jurist, 1995). Movement into new areas during late summer and early autumn may be partially the result of exploratory activity (Cryan, 2003). Thus, the temporal pattern of bat collision mortality in the region simply may be related to increased bat activity before and during migration, with corresponding increases in encounters with wind turbines.

Researchers should use caution when attempting to extrapolate data of bat behavior collected from ground level (acoustical data and mist-netting) to behavior at turbine rotor heights, that is, beyond the range of bat call detectors placed on the ground (Furlonger et al., 1987). Ground level mist-netting and acoustic monitoring are inherently biased (Menzel et al., 1999). If resident bats rarely hit turbines during non-migratory periods (Johnson et al., 2004; this study) then the increase in ultrasonic activity detected at ground level during migratory periods may indicate that turbine collision may not occur during migratory flight, but rather as a result of increased activity related to dispersal, migration and staging. Such activities would bring migrant bats within range of ground based detectors. Future studies on site location and mitigation of fatalities due to wind turbines should quantify the relationship between bat activity at various heights and determine how often bats echolocate while migrating and flying around turbines.

Winkelman (1994) and Horn (2004) observed that the turbulence in the wake of wind turbines was powerful enough to buffet birds and bats. Similarly, fatalities due to internal hemorrhaging as described by Baerwald et al. (2008) are also possible without contact with the turbine or blades. Similar studies involving observation by use of ultrasonic bat data and thermal video at ground, supra-canopy and blade levels at WRAs and during pre-development surveys could describe which bat species use the area around wind turbines and how bats use echolocation in situations at turbine height. These data should be compared with rigorous carcass search protocols at frequencies adequate to attribute individual fatality events to observed activity and specific weather events (Cryan and Brown, 2007; Arnett et al., 2008). The comparatively higher fatality rates of non-migratory species at this wind farm indicates that future research should not ignore the possibility of population level effects for these species. Little brown bats currently suffer massive fatality rates from white-nose syndrome (Blehert et al., 2009), and are likely unable to sustain population levels, even without wind turbine related

fatalities. There is a lack of adequate background data on bat populations and habits. While new wind farm locations are chosen, multiple season studies on both local and migrant bat populations and their flight patterns remain necessary.
